paras: The lynching of Ed Reeves was the killing of a Black man by a mob in Ballard County, Kentucky, in mid-August 1881, after he was accused of an attempted assault on a woman in Graves County. Captured in Ballard County, he was taken from the men bringing him to the Graves County jail and, by most accounts, hanged. The story reached papers from Pennsylvania to Georgia as a short wire item, headed in some of them 'A BRUTE LYNCHED'.

According to a special dispatch from Paducah, Reeves, described as 'colored', was accused of breaking into the room of Miss Dora Lingston in Graves County at night on August 9 and attempting 'indecent violence'. Her cries brought help, he fled, and 'the whole country swarmed with pursuers'. An Ohio rewrite of the story said he was pursued by 'a body of men who were determined to lynch him if captured'.

Reeves was captured in Ballard County, at Ogden's Landing according to the Paducah special, or in 'the lowlands of Ballard County' according to the Ohio version. The special said that a 'large mounted mob' took him from 'the persons conducting him to the Graves county jail' and lynched him, and the Ohio version said a mob met 'the authorities' on the road and seized the prisoner. A brief in the New Hampshire Patriot reported that he was 'hung by lynchers' in Ballard County on Tuesday, which was August 16.

The Daily Cairo Bulletin of Cairo, Illinois, printed a different version. It named the captors as A. J. Cunn and Wm. Harper, who found Reeves at the house of a man named Ford and soon turned him over to a party of men searching for him. The Bulletin did not confirm the killing, saying only that 'it is believed' the men hanged him to a tree before leaving Ballard County.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and none of the papers named members of the mob.

White papers carried the story as a brief, mostly from the Paducah special, which the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer printed on August 17 with the state given wrongly as Tennessee. The Washington Evening Star ran it on August 18 under 'A BRUTE LYNCHED', and the Savannah Morning News reprinted the same text on August 23. Each version stated the accusation as fact, and the New Hampshire Patriot listed the lynching among crime news as punishment 'for assault on a white woman'.

On August 25 two Ohio weeklies, the Somerset Press and the Eaton Democrat, printed a rewritten paragraph headed 'Sudden Transition' that spelled the name 'Reines' and the woman's name 'Langston'. The Cairo Bulletin called Reeves 'the scoundrel' and 'the wretch' and reported the handover to the searchers without comment. No paper in the coverage questioned the lynching.

Accounts differ on how Reeves passed to the mob: the Paducah special and the Ohio rewrite describe a seizure from an escort, while the Cairo Bulletin says his captors handed him over. They also differ on the killing, which the wire reports state outright and the Cairo Bulletin gives only as belief.

reader.title: Lynching of Ed Reeves
bases: A mob took a Black man accused of an attempted assault on a white woman from his captors and, by most reports, hanged him (A2, A3, A6), with one regional paper reporting the hanging only as belief (A4).

The Paducah special and the Ohio rewrite say a 'large mounted mob' or 'a mob' took Reeves from those taking him to jail and lynched him, and a New Hampshire brief says he was 'hung by lynchers' for assault on a white woman (A2, A3, A6); the Cairo Bulletin reports the hanging only as what 'is believed' (A4).

The Paducah wire special (A1, A2) and the separately sourced Cairo Bulletin (A4) agree on the accusation, the capture in Ballard county and the handover to a party of men, and the special and A3 state the lynching outright, though A4 hedges on the killing.

accounts.label: Paducah special (wire)
accounts.gist: Reeves broke into Miss Lingston's room on August 9, fled when her cries brought help, was captured at Ogden's Landing, and was taken by a large mounted mob from the persons conducting him to the Graves county jail and lynched.

accounts.label: Cairo Bulletin (regional)
accounts.gist: Cunn and Harper captured Reeves at Ford's house in Ballard county and shortly after turned him over to men searching for him, who it was believed hanged him to a tree before leaving Ballard county.

accounts.label: Ohio rewrite ('Sudden Transition')
accounts.gist: Pursued by men determined to lynch him, Reines was arrested by the authorities in the Ballard County lowlands and seized by a mob that met them on the way to the Graves County jail.

framing.detail: The wire special ran under 'A BRUTE LYNCHED', stating the accusation as fact and the lynching without comment.
The Cairo Bulletin called Reeves 'the scoundrel' and 'the wretch' and reported his handover to the searchers without criticism.

Northern papers ran short briefs among crime news: 'captured and lynched' in Lancaster, 'hung by lynchers' in Concord, and a 'Sudden Transition' item in Ohio weeklies that stated he 'committed an assault'.
